metadata.title: Michael Burry warns of 1987-style crash, holds Nvidia shorts

content.text:
Michael Burry warned Tuesday that the S&P 500's surge to a record high could precede a sharp decline similar to the 1987 stock-market crash, while maintaining short positions in Nvidia, the iShares Semiconductor ETF, Micron, Caterpillar, Palantir, Tesla, and Applied Materials.
"I continue to believe it is possible we are near a major top, and possible a 1987-type fall, but the S&P 500 making new highs likely will bring new money into the market," Burry wrote in a Tuesday Substack post.
The S&P 500 climbed 1.9% Tuesday, notching its first record close since June, as solid corporate earnings and declining oil prices — amid optimism that the Strait of Hormuz could reopen — lifted sentiment. The Nasdaq Composite gained 2.7%.
Burry argued the rally contains a self-reinforcing dynamic. "Remember, the market going up on falling volatility forces vol-targeting funds to leverage up, and brings leverage from other momentum strategies into play," he wrote. He also noted that the S&P 500 has surged 5% over four trading days to a new high only three other times, citing analysis from Jonathan Krinsky at BTIG — once in March 2000, once in April 1999, and once in November 2020.
Despite the broad market advance, Burry said all of his short positions remain profitable except his bet against Nvidia stock. He noted, however, that a decisive move against any of his trades would prompt him to close out those positions. "Again, shorting is not for everyone," he wrote. "I must short. Most should not."
Burry has long been skeptical of the AI investment cycle, contending that the capital flowing into AI infrastructure relies on funding structures that could eventually buckle, according to CNBC.
Burry's position on several of the names dates back further. He held put options on Palantir and added to his Nvidia short position earlier this year, buying January 2027 puts on Nvidia with a $115 strike price at $3.30 per contract. At the time, he described Palantir as "wildly overvalued" and set his fundamental value for the company at well under $50 per share.
Black Monday — the name given to the 1987 crash — unfolded on October 19 of that year, when the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 22.6% of its value in a single session, a one-day loss unmatched in the index's history, according to Benzinga. The rout quickly crossed borders into international markets, with program trading, widespread panic among investors, and thin liquidity all cited as contributing factors, according to Benzinga.
